title: High Social Media Use Raises Mental Health Risks in Teens. A Landmark Australian Study Just Quantified the Damage.
excerpt: A population-based cohort of 13-to-16-year-olds shows heavy social media use is linked to depression, anxiety and cyberbullying — and a separate trial found that just cutting back reduces loneliness within weeks.
body:
The debate over whether social media harms teenagers has been long on alarm and short on rigour. Two new studies, one from Australia and one from Canada, have just supplied the kind of evidence that turns the argument from speculation into science — and for diaspora parents managing screen time across two cultural contexts, the findings demand attention.

The first, published in the *Medical Journal of Australia* in June 2026, is a population-based cohort study led by researchers at the Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) in Melbourne. It tracked 13-to-16-year-olds who actively use platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube, measuring their mental health outcomes alongside their digital behaviours.

The findings are not ambiguous. High levels of social media use were associated with increased rates of depression, anxiety, cyberbullying exposure and contact with harmful online content. Professor Susan Sawyer of MCRI put it plainly: "Our results don't suggest that social media is universally harmful, but it's not without some harms."

## The Numbers Behind the Noise

Nearly three-quarters of adolescents in Australia now experience clinically significant depression or anxiety symptoms, according to prior MCRI research — a figure so high that it demands structural explanations beyond individual vulnerability.

The new study fills that gap. It identifies social media intensity — measured not just by screen time but by frequency of engagement, types of content consumed and extent of social comparison — as a significant predictor of poor mental health outcomes. Teens with the highest usage reported more cyberbullying, more exposure to content promoting self-harm or eating disorders, and higher rates of anxiety than their lower-usage peers.

What the study does not find is equally important. It does not conclude that social media is uniformly toxic. Many adolescents reported positive experiences around social belonging, self-expression and identity exploration. The harm concentrates at the high end of the usage spectrum, suggesting that intensity matters far more than mere presence on a platform.

## The Canadian Trial: Proof That Cutting Back Works

If the Australian data establishes the problem, a randomised controlled trial from Canada offers the prescription.

Published in the *Journal of Affective Disorders* in June 2026, the study by Gary Goldfield and colleagues at the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario recruited youth already diagnosed with anxiety and depression. Participants were randomised to either reduce their social media use or continue as usual.

The results were striking. Those who cut back experienced significant reductions in loneliness — and the effect held regardless of gender or the degree to which participants engaged in social comparison. The finding is critical because it demonstrates causality: reducing social media use did not merely correlate with feeling less lonely, it produced the improvement.

For a generation told that connection is just a tap away, the irony is profound. The platforms designed to bring people closer together are, at high doses, making the most vulnerable among them feel more isolated.

## Why Diaspora Parents Should Pay Attention

For Indian-origin families in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, these findings land in especially complicated territory.

Many diaspora parents already navigate a cultural tightrope around technology. South Asian parenting norms tend to emphasise academic discipline and structured time, but the social fabric of Western schools runs through group chats, Instagram stories and TikTok trends. Restricting access too aggressively risks social isolation; permitting it without guardrails risks the harms the data now documents.

Australia has already acted. In December 2025, the country introduced age restrictions on social media access for teenagers, and MCRI researchers are now monitoring the impact through the Connected Minds Study. No equivalent legislation exists in the United States, where platforms remain largely self-regulated.

The practical guidance from both studies converges on three points. First, total usage matters: the harms escalate with intensity, so setting daily time limits is a defensible intervention. Second, content type matters: passive scrolling and social comparison are more damaging than active creation and direct messaging. Third, the intervention works: even modest reductions in social media use produce measurable improvements in loneliness and mood among teens who are already struggling.

## What Families Can Do Now

Researchers recommend age-appropriate limits, better digital literacy education and clearer parental guidance — the kind of structured approach that many South Asian families are culturally inclined to provide, if given the evidence to justify it.

The evidence has arrived. The question now is whether families will use it before the algorithms use their children.
